Animal bites to the hands should receive antibiotic prophylaxis (see ). A
Prophylactic antibiotics for dog and cat bites for other body areas are commonly given although no evidence supports this practice. C

background.definition: Dog and cat bites disrupt the skin causing mechanical damage and create potential wound infections.

list.listitem: More than 800,000 medical visits for dog bites annually, approximately 370,000 of which are emergency department visits.
Cat bites resulted in more than 66,000 emergency department visit per year from 2001 to 2004.
Younger children have higher incidence of facial bites than do older children and adults.
In a series of 704 patients with 765 dog bites, 26.7% were on the head/neck, 20.4% on the hand, 15.7% on the arm, 10.1% on the trunk, 25.4% on the thigh or leg, and 1.7% on the foot.
Dog and cat bites may come from unprovoked (higher risk of rabies) or provoked (including feeding, petting or touching) animals that may be domesticated or feral.

Two systematic reviews found the highest severe biting risk with mixed breed dogs and Pit Bulls, followed by German Shephards and Jack Russell terriers. Labrador and golden retrievers, cocker spaniels, and border collies had an intermediate risk.
Mechanical disruption and crushing of skin and deeper structures by the bite can cause significant cosmetic damage and functional loss.
Because of the puncture wounds associated with teeth and the animal's oral flora, significant wound infections can result.
Pasteurella species are associated with 50% of dog and 75% of cat bites.
Mixed aerobic and anaerobic infection is present in 56% of wounds.
Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and anaerobes such as Bacteroides are also common.
Capnocytophaga canimorsus, a Gram-negative rod, can cause serious and sometimes fatal sepsis in asplenic patients.

A Cochrane review concluded that although there is no direct evidence that educational programs for children reduce dog and cat bites, education for children who are younger than 10 years in school settings could improve their knowledge, attitude, and behavior toward dogs. B
Upon presentation, obtain personal health history, especially if asplenic or immune-suppressed, and details about biting animal to determine need for tetanus and/or rabies prophylaxis. C

Ask about the cause and time of bite, its location, status of animal (known/unknown, in captivity), personal health history especially if asplenic or immune-suppressed, medication allergies, and tetanus status. Examine the bite wound and assess for complicating injury such as fracture, tendon or tendon sheath injury, or possible joint involvement.
Infections from bites can occur within 24 to 72 hours.
Do a thorough physical examination of affected body part including circulation, sensation and functional status.
Consider radiographs of the affected areas to rule out fractures or foreign bodies (eg, teeth) in the soft tissues.
Obtain wound cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) if evidence of infection at presentation. Many times, these are not necessary as empiric antibiotic therapy is commonly used.
Aggressive irrigation, cleansing, and debridement are mandatory.
Most bite wounds should not have primary closure due to infection potential.
Determine if antibiotic prophylaxis is warranted.
Determine if rabies prophylaxis is warranted (see chapter on Rabies).
Determine if tetanus prophylaxis is warranted (see ).
Aggressive local care with copious irrigation and debridement of devitalized tissues is imperative. C
Bites to the hand should receive antibiotic prophylaxis, regardless of severity or depth. A
Prophylactic antibiotics for bites for other body areas are commonly given, although no evidence supports this practice. C

Primary closure may be attempted in low-risk populations (within 8 hours of injury, especially on the face where risk of infection is low and cosmesis is important). Otherwise, allow wound to close by secondary intention. B

Antibiotic prophylaxis directed against most common causative organisms (Pasteurella, Streptococci, Staphylococci, and anaerobes) is commonly recommended for cat bites and most dog bites (see ). Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125 mg twice each day for 3 to 5 days is the preferred empiric therapy.

Current guidelines recommend early antimicrobial therapy for 3 to 5 days for patients who are immunocompromised, asplenic, have advanced liver disease, have preexisting or resultant edema of the affected area, have moderate to severe injuries especially to the hand or face, or have injuries that may have penetrated the periosteum or joint capsule.

Tetanus toxoid should be administered to patients without toxoid vaccination within 10 years. Tetanus, diptheria, and pertussis (Tdap) is preferred over Tetanus and diptheria (Td) if the former has not been previously given.

Evidence of benefit is mixed. One systematic review found a benefit of antibiotic prophylaxis (OR 0.56; 95% CI, 0.38-0.82; NNT 14). On the other hand, a Cochrane systematic review of 8 RCTs found no reduction in the rate of infection except in hand bites (OR 0.10; 95% CI, 0.01-0.86; NNT 4).

If rabies are suspected, give rabies immunoglobulin as a single dose of 20 IU/kg, divided between bite areas (if possible) and gluteal area. This can be given up to 7 days after a bite. Suspect rabies in an unprovoked attack by an animal with abnormal behavior, signs of illness, or obvious/unexplained wound (petting, feeding, or touching an animal is considered provocation). A dog or cat with up-to-date immunizations is unlikely to become infected with rabies.
Give rabies virus vaccination 1 mL IM on days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28 after a suspicious bite. Also give tetanus prophylaxis, if indicated (see ).

Evidence of necrosis or nonviable tissue requires aggressive local wound care/debridement with exposure/exploration of entire extent of the wound and debridement to the level of bleeding tissue. Sequential debridement may be required if unable to fully assess degree of devitalization.
A retrospective review of 111 patients who suffered either a dog or cat bite to the hand found that approximately 1/3 of patients required at least 1 surgical procedure.
The need for bacteriocidal/virucidal irrigation agent (eg, povidone iodine) is controversial—many advocate clean tap water or sterile water.
Consider allowing closure by secondary intention for most dog and cat bite wounds due to infection potential.
Consider primary closure if low risk of infection (shallow laceration, location on the face or trunk, without puncture or involvement of deep structures, within 8 hours of bite).
A Cochrane review of 3 RCTs involving 878 patients found no high-certainty evidence to support or refute primary closure of traumatic wounds from dog bites.
Based upon severity of injury, requirement for surgical intervention, extent of devitalized/injured tissues.
Moderate pressure irrigation of at least 150 mL solution with 20 to 35 mL syringe with 18 to 20 gauge angiocatheter is recommended.
Pulsatile jet lavage (50-70 psi) should be reserved for grossly soiled wounds as it can lead to tissue disruption.

Referral is recommended if there is a need for surgical exploration (eg, involvement of deeper structures on the hands, more extensive debridement or repair required to repair wound, evidence of persistent infection not responding to oral antibiotics).
Approximately 3% to 18% of dog bites become infected, as do 28% to 80% of cat bites. B
Predictors of wound infection include age older than 50 years, full thickness wound, female gender, and need for wound debridement. B
Close follow-up within 24 to 48 hours is indicated for reevaluation for evidence of infection; monitor for signs of infection throughout duration of antibiotic prophylaxis/treatment. C
Risk of infection is higher in patients with chronic edema of the affected area, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, liver dysfunction, prosthetic joint, prosthetic heart valve, or splenectomy.

feature.caption: Tetanus Prophylaxis Recommendations.
feature.feature_body:
Clean, minor wounds All other wounds*
History of tetanus toxoid vaccination TDAP, TD, or DTAP† TIG TDAP, TD, or DTAP† TIG§
Unknown or less than 3 doses Yes No Yes Yes
Greater than 3 doses No¶ No No No**
*Such as, but not limited to, wounds contaminated with dirt, feces, soil, and saliva; puncture wounds; avulsions; and wounds resulting from missiles, crushing, burns, and frostbite. †DTaP is recommended for children aged <7 years. Tdap is preferred to Td for persons aged ≥11 years who have not previously received Tdap. Persons aged ≥7 years who are not fully immunized against pertussis, tetanus or diphtheria should receive one dose of Tdap for wound management and as part of the catch-up series. § Persons with HIV infection or severe immunodeficiency who have contaminated wounds should also receive TIG, regardless of their history of tetanus immunization. ¶Yes, if >10 years since the last tetanus toxoid–containing vaccine dose. ** Yes, if ≥5 years since the last tetanus toxoid–containing vaccine dose. From: Prevention of Pertussis, Tetanus, and Diphtheria with Vaccines in the United States: Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP). MMWR. April 27, 2018.
